hook: You know Jesus said “It is finished” as he died. But did you know it is one word in Greek, and John has already used it two verses before?
story:
In John’s Gospel these are the last words Jesus speaks before he dies: “It is finished!” Then “he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.” The other Gospels end differently. In Luke the last cry is “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” Matthew and Mark tell of a loud cry and give no words for it. In John, this is the last.

Heard on its own, it can sound like a man at the end of his strength. That’s it, it’s over. Did Jesus give up?

Look at the word. In Greek it is one word, tetelestai, from the verb teleo: to finish, to bring something to its end. And John has used it two verses earlier. Before Jesus says “I am thirsty!”, John tells us he was “seeing that all things were now finished”. The same word. John lets us know what Jesus knew before Jesus says it out loud. John does not say that his life was finished. He says all things were.

The night before, Jesus had prayed to his Father, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do.” Long before, sitting by a well in Samaria, he had told his disciples, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” Gary Manning, who teaches New Testament at Biola University, notes that these verses use a closely related word, and that John has made his readers wait all along for Jesus to finish the task the Father gave him.

Even the verb for gave up says something. It is the verb John used a few verses earlier for Pilate, who “delivered him to them to be crucified.” Pilate handed Jesus over. Now Jesus hands over his spirit.

moment:
It is the Preparation Day, near the city, at the place called Golgotha. The soldiers have divided his clothes into four parts and cast lots for the seamless tunic. Near the cross stand his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene, and the disciple whom he loved.

Jesus speaks to them first. To his mother: “Woman, behold, your son!” To the disciple: “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, John says, the disciple took her to his own home.

Then, knowing that all was finished, he says “I am thirsty!” A vessel of vinegar is standing there. They fill a sponge with it, put it on hyssop and hold it to his mouth. He takes it, and he speaks once more.

John tells the next moments carefully. Jesus bows his head, and then he gives up his spirit. When the soldiers come to break the legs of the crucified, so that the bodies can be taken down before the Sabbath, they find that he is “already dead”. John adds a line about the one who saw it all: “He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true.”
around:
The whole scene is full of Scripture coming true. The soldiers cast lots for his clothing, “that the Scripture might be fulfilled”, and John quotes the psalm: “They parted my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing.” Jesus says he is thirsty so that another Scripture would be fulfilled, and Augustine connected it with the psalm that says, “In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink.” Afterwards John quotes two more: “A bone of him will not be broken” and “They will look on him whom they pierced.”

Earlier in the Gospel Jesus had said of his life, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself.” Luke records him saying, long before the cross, “how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” Thayer’s Greek lexicon lists that verb, too, under teleo. And at the start of the last night, John wrote that Jesus “loved them to the end.” On the cross, the end has come.
after:
John’s story does not stop at the tomb. On the first day of the week Mary Magdalene comes to the disciples with the news “that she had seen the Lord”.

The letter to the Hebrews puts the finished work in a picture. It says that Christ, “when he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God”: a work done, and a seat taken.

Over the centuries the saying became one of the seven words from the cross, a tradition that arranges the sayings of all four Gospels in one order, with this one as the sixth. Since the sixteenth century those sayings have been widely used in sermons on Good Friday, and in the Three Hours’ devotion, held from noon to three, the hours of the darkness in Matthew, Mark and Luke.

Preachers kept returning to the word itself. On 1 December 1861 Charles Spurgeon preached on this verse in London and pointed out that it occurs twice within three verses. Leo the Great and Martin Luther, Gary Manning notes, heard in it both a finished work and fulfilled Scripture.
readings:
Christians have heard several things in the one word, and they often hold them together.

A finished task. Jesus came to do the Father’s work, and now it is done.

Fulfilled Scripture. John frames the word with Scripture being fulfilled. Augustine asked what was finished and answered: all that prophecy had foretold so long before. Leo the Great and Martin Luther saw both meanings at once, and Gary Manning writes that this double reading, the work and the Scripture, is found in almost all modern commentaries on John.

A debt paid. Many Christians hear paid in full in it. The verb can mean to pay when it is used with taxes, as when the collectors ask Peter, “Doesn’t your teacher pay the didrachma?”, and in Paul’s line, “you also pay taxes”. The claim that receipts of the time were marked with this word is disputed. The belief that Christ paid for sin rests on other passages as well.

A death freely given. Ellicott’s commentary notes that all the words used for this death stress that it was voluntary, and Augustine marveled at a man who died when he chose.

And there is the question of the different last words. Many churches join the sayings of the four Gospels into seven words. Others read each Gospel on its own; Michael Licona, for example, suggests that John gives Jesus’ final words in a simpler form of his own. Both start from the same texts.
argued:
For a time the debt reading seemed to have evidence on its side. Gary Manning tells the story. Tax receipts from Egypt were published in 1896, and in 1915 an important Greek reference book, Moulton and Milligan’s Vocabulary of the Greek Testament, connected the word on them with Jesus’ cry. From there the idea reached many pulpits.

Long before that, preachers had spoken of the cross as a debt paid. Charles Spurgeon did so in 1861, in his sermon on this verse: [[spurgeon-debt]]

Manning, writing a commentary on John, went back to the papyri themselves, about 315 tax receipts. He found that almost all of them carry only an abbreviation, and where the clerks wrote the word out in full, it was a different word, meaning paid as taxes. He also looked at how the word of John 19:30 is used in other documents: [[manning]]

So Manning sets the receipts aside and keeps what he finds in John’s own setting, the reading that Leo the Great and Luther shared: [[manning-double]]

Many Christians still hear a debt paid in this cry, as Spurgeon did, and that belief never depended on the receipts. Manning’s point is narrower: the word itself did not mean paid in full.
point: Without John’s own frame, “It is finished!” can sound like surrender. With it, it means the opposite. John says Jesus knew all things were finished before he said so, he uses the same word for both, and he tells the death as an act: Jesus bows his head and hands over his spirit. The cry is not the end of a man who lost. It is the word of someone whose task is complete.
lesson:
There is a difference between the runner who collapses before the line and the runner who crosses it and says: done. John wants you to see the second.

That matters for how you come to God. If the work Jesus came to do is finished, you are not asked to complete it, only to receive it. Many people live as if faith were a debt they must keep paying off, never sure it is enough. The word from the cross speaks into that: what he came to do, he finished.

It also gives you a way to look at your own unfinished days. Jesus spoke of finishing the work the Father had given him. You can ask the same about your life: not whether you did everything, but whether you did what was given to you.

Read John 17 and John 19 one evening, side by side, and listen for the word finished. And if you do not share this faith, you can still notice what John wanted his readers to see: in his telling, Jesus does not die defeated.

echoes.note: At the creation, “God finished his work which he had done; and he rested”. In John, Jesus finishes the work the Father gave him, and the next day is a Sabbath.
Hebrews says what a finished work means for others: “For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.”
Many Christians hear a debt settled in Jesus’ last word in John. Paul speaks of “the handwriting in ordinances which was against us”, taken out of the way and nailed “to the cross.”
Paul uses the same verb for his own life near its end: “I have finished the course.” A follower can close his life with the word his Lord used on the cross.
